title: Weqatal

objectives.can: Recognise weqatal and read it as continuing a future, a command or a habitual action.

explanation.summary: Weqatal is the qatal form with the conjunction וְ in front, used to carry on from a verb that came before it: a command, a future event, a general statement or a repeated action. It is the counterpart of wayyiqtol, but it shows itself less clearly, so you learn it by context as much as by shape.

sections.heading: What the form looks like
body: A weqatal verb is a qatal verb with the ordinary conjunction attached: וְאָהַבְתָּ, וְהָיוּ, וְדָבַק. The conjunction is וְ, or וּ before a letter with shewa, such as וּקְשַׁרְתָּם. Unlike the wayyiqtol, nothing is doubled and the vowel under the waw is the ordinary one.

So on the page a weqatal and a qatal with a plain 'and' are the same shape. Which one you have depends on how the verb is used. The analysed text records its own decision: it labels one verb weqatal and another qatal with a prefix, and you will see both in the examples. That label is the edition's analysis, and a reader should treat it as the tradition's reading of the sentence rather than something the letters prove.

Grammarians also describe a movement of the stress to the last syllable in some first person singular and second masculine singular forms. It shows only in the accent signs, which this course leaves out of its tables and questions, and it does not decide the label.

sections.heading: Continuing a command, a future or a general statement
body: The weqatal rarely stands at the head of a passage. It continues a verb before it and takes its time-frame from that verb. If the verb before is an imperative, the weqatal usually continues the command, 'do this, and do that'. If it is a yiqtol that looks to the future or describes what always happens, the weqatal does the same. If it is a participle meaning 'is about to', the weqatal adds the next thing that will happen.

That is why laws and instructions are full of weqatal. A chain of weqatals in the second person is a series of things the hearer is to do, as in the passage you read at the end of this lesson. English usually renders the chain with 'you shall … and you shall …', or with a series of commands.

sections.heading: Continuing a repeated action in the past
body: The same pattern works in the past when the description is of a habit or repeated event. A yiqtol sets the habit ('Moses would take the tent') and weqatal verbs carry on in the same frame ('and would pitch it'). English handles this with 'would' or 'used to'. It is a different use from the wayyiqtol chain of a story, which tells things that happened once, one after another.
The conjunction can also give a weqatal an introductory role: וְהָיָה, 'and it will be', opens a statement of what will happen or what usually happens whenever something occurs.

sections.heading: Why a form like this? A view and an older view
body: The older grammars describe the weqatal as a perfect 'converted' to a future or an imperfect by the waw, in parallel with the 'waw conversive' of the wayyiqtol. A common modern description does not treat the waw as converting anything: it says that the weqatal carries on the mood and time-frame already set in the context. Both descriptions fit the same texts, and this course reads the form by its use.

misunderstandings: A weqatal is not a past tense because it is built on the qatal. In most of its uses it points forward in time, or describes what is general or repeated.
Every qatal with וְ in front is not a weqatal. A plain conjunction before a qatal often just adds a past event or a clause. The label depends on the sentence.
Do not translate every weqatal with 'and'. The English 'shall', 'will' or 'would' is usually what the context needs.
Weqatal does not tell a story by itself. A story is carried on by wayyiqtol. When weqatal appears in narrative it is usually a habitual or repeated action.

deeper.heading: Who decides the label?
body: For some verses the sources differ: an edition may count a verb as weqatal and another as a plain qatal. The analysed text used here follows one tradition, and where its label surprises you, look at the verb before it and at the sense. That is the same decision the Hebrew reader has to make.

examples.analysis: A general statement. יַעֲזָב is a yiqtol: it states what a man does, as a rule. וְדָבַק, 'and he clings', and וְהָיוּ, 'and they become', are weqatal and continue the same statement. They are not events in a story: the verse describes what marriage is.

examples.analysis: A repeated event in the past. וְהָיָה begins the account of what used to happen whenever Moses went out. The yiqtol יָקוּמוּ and the weqatals וְנִצְּבוּ, 'and they would stand', and וְהִבִּיטוּ, 'and they would look', describe a habit, not a single occasion. The weqatals are in Niphal and Hiphil.
